newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE-Battles flare over Philippine oil market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Battles flare over Philippine oil market.

text.p: Had the Philippine peso weakened any further, it would have taken more than Batman and Robin and a model Ferrari for the country's major oil refiners to keep the competiton at bay, analysts and oil company officials say.

Since February's sweeping deregulation of the industry, oil firms have started to get big on promotions, after discovering that television advertisements were no longer enough to entice the public to drive to their filling stations.
Caltex Philippines Inc started the ball rolling by sponsoring the Manila premiere of the newly released "Star Wars". It then launched the country's first co-funded credit card for loyal customers.
Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp began handing out costly miniature Ferrari models to customers who garner points from fuel purchases plus a small payment.
Not to be left out, Petron Corp sponsored the debut of another hit film, "Batman & Robin".
"GUERRILLA TACTICS"
The oil refiners, who for so long dominated a now booming Philippine market, have taken competition to heart.

"New entrants have resorted to guerrilla tactics giving as big a discount as they can. They are mostly hitting on commercial accounts -- companies like the National Power Corp -- where it is easiest to penetrate," said Frank Cruz, vice-president for logistics at Caltex Philippines.
Data from the Department of Energy showed that for the first quarter of the year alone, three percent of the market, or about 10,000 barrels of oil a day, was captured by new entrants.
These newcomers were expected to grab about 10 percent of retail business in the next five years, an oil firm official said.
With newcomers snapping at their heels, oil refiners said the last thing they needed was a weak peso to push up prices.
FOREIGN EXCHANGE LOSSES
Just over a week ago, the government finally caved in to a wave of speculative attacks and allowed a de facto devaluation of the peso.
For local oil refiners who import all their crude, a weaker peso meant a higher landed cost of crude and foreign exchange losses due to dollar-denominated debts.

"Of course, the new entrants will be in the same boat as we are but they do not have as much foreign exchange losses as we do. Despite the peso's comeback, we were already hit," said one company official.
As a result, he said the new companies may be in a slightly stronger position.
Oil company executives estimate that a one peso ($0.03) depreciation against the dollar will translate into a 13 to 14 centavo increase per litre of petroleum products sold by local oil refiners.
CARRYING THE COST
So far, the oil firms have not adjusted prices, partly under strong pressure from business to keep prices down despite the peso's fall of just over six percent.
Leading businessman and the chairman of a task force on power, Raul Concepcion, noted that oil firms had two months' worth of stocks and did not need to put up prices.
"The fuel we have right now we indeed bought 60 days ago but we have not paid for it and we will be carrying the cost of a weaker peso," countered an oil company official.

"The government is using strong moral suasion and Petron is very big on that. Without Petron moving, we can't move. I don't know how many days we can afford (not to raise prices)," said another company executive.
If an oil refiner adjusts its prices without the others following, it will mean a loss in market share for the company that initiated the increase.
Petron, partly owned by Saudi Arabia's Aramco and the state-run Philippine National Oil Co, has emerged as the price setter since the market was deregulated.

Anscor-Hagedorn Securities' vice-president, Noel Reyes, said: "We basically have three Goliaths and 13 dwarfs. These big oil firms can cope with the emerging ones. They will pass on costs brought about by the peso's fall. They just have public opinion to contend with."
